extracted.intended_audience: Members of Parliament, policymakers, and the learned public concerned with press licencing and freedom of learning
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay arguing against statutory licencing/censorship of printed books, detailing practical, moral, and political objections and describing what a licencing regime would require and how it would harm learning and liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencer must be infallible and uncorrupt
rubrics_metrics.description: The licencer must be entrusted with authority 'unlesse we can conferr upon them... the grace of infallibility, and uncorruptednesse', otherwise their judgment cannot be relied on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that to censor safely you'd need licencers whose judgement is beyond question — an unrealistic standard. Anti-pattern: appointing ordinary men and expecting perfect judgement; consequence: mis-censures and suppression of valuable thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencer must be studious, learned, and judicious
rubrics_metrics.description: He who is made judge to sit upon the birth, or death of books 'had need to be a man above the common measure, both studious, learned, and judicious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection criteria for a licencer are very high; otherwise 'mean mistakes' and severe injury will result. Practical guidance: if you cannot staff licencing with such persons, the regime is ill-advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing requires exhaustive review of all books and pamphlets
rubrics_metrics.description: The licencer would be 'the perpetuall reader of unchosen books and pamphlets, oftimes huge volumes' and must read at all times, creating a huge, tedious burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feasibility metric: count of materials to review, reading time, and inspector capacity. Anti-pattern: treating cursory review as sufficient; result: careless or remiss censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing must also regulate other corrupting influences
rubrics_metrics.description: If you regulate printing to rectify manners, you must 'regulat all recreations and pastimes... No musick must be heard... there must be licencing dancers... who shall silence all the airs and madrigalls... the Windows also, and the Balcone's must be thought on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensiveness requirement: either accept partial, ineffective censorship or undertake an impossible all-encompassing moral police. The essay uses this to show impracticality and absurd scope creep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books cannot be suppressed without damaging learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Those books which are likeliest to taint life and doctrine 'cannot be suppresst without the fall of learning, and of all ability in disputation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy trade-off: suppression of controversial works will undermine scholarly debate and the capacity to dispute and refine ideas. Scoring: negative for measures that reduce the corpus of disputable texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial expurgation demands skilled officials for nuanced edits
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 'books which are partly usefull and excellent, partly culpable and pernicious; this work will ask as many more officials, to make expurgations, and expunctions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational requirement: ability to excise offending passages without destroying usefulness. Anti-pattern: blunt bans rather than careful redaction; consequence: loss of valuable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing ineffective against schisms and religious error
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent sects and schisms by licencing is futile: many sects 'refusing books as a hindrance' preserved doctrine by unwritten tradition and licencing did not stop schisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness criterion: historical evidence shows banning books does not prevent sectarianism. Use this as a measure of policy impact on religious conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement must be complete or the order is fruitless
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If execution be remisse or blindfold... what will it be hereafter and in other books? ... then the order shall not be vain and frustrat.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement quality metric: incomplete enforcement renders licencing pointless. Consider costs of achieving truly comprehensive enforcement vs. likely gaps and circumventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing discourages learned men and affronts learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The order is 'the greatest discouragement and affront, that can be offer'd to learning and to learned men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural impact metric: measure how policy affects recruitment, morale, and reputation of scholars. Negative scores for measures that demean or infantilize competent authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenser's office will attract inferior, negligent, or venal appointees
rubrics_metrics.description: If the burden is excessive 'none that is not a plain unthrift of his own hours is ever likely to succeed them, except he mean to put himself to the salary of a Presse-corrector' — thus future licencers will be 'ignorant, imperious, and remisse, or basely pecuniary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk assessment: poor staffing will corrupt the regime. Criterion: evaluate incentives and likelihood of appointing qualified, conscientious licencers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing causes practical delays and freezes printing
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' last-minute insertions cannot be added because 'The Printer dares not go beyond his licenc't copy... either the Presse must stand still ... or the author loose his accuratest thoughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness metric: measure how licencing slows publication and prevents iterative improvements. Negative for hampering authorship fluidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing is a dishonour and infantilization of authors
rubrics_metrics.description: If serious writings must 'not be utter'd without the cursory eyes of a temporizing and extemporizing licencer... he who is not trusted with his own actions... has no great argument to think himself reputed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect metric: policies should avoid publicly diminishing an author's standing. Anti-pattern: mandatory censors' signatures on titles signalling paternal oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing risks reintroducing episcopal or arbitrary authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The order may be 'a second tyranny over learning' and 'translate the Palace Metropolitan from one kind of dominion into another' — a political consolidation risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political-risk criterion: assess whether censorship mechanisms concentrate ecclesiastical or state power and reverse prior reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment and prohibition can enhance the authority of writers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The punishing of wits enhaunces their autority ... a forbidd'n writing is thought to be a certain spark of truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backfire metric: censorship may make censured works more attractive and authoritative. Account for counterproductive publicity effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of printing is necessary for the exercise and growth of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth 'thrives by exercise... Truth is compar'd in Scripture to a streaming fountain; if her waters flow not... they sick'n into a muddy pool of conformity and tradition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principled criterion: openness enables debate and verification. Policies should preserve channels for public disputation and continual testing of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing infantilizes the public by implying they cannot read without a licencer
rubrics_metrics.description: If we 'dare not trust' the people with an English pamphlet, we 'but censure them for a giddy, vitious, and ungrounded people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-autonomy metric: avoid policies that treat citizens as incapable of judgement; consider civic consequences of patronizing censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing cannot stop oral or teacher-led propagation of error
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil doctrine 'not with books can propagate, except a teacher guide, which he might also doe without writing' — oral transmission undermines book suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness test: measure how policy addresses non-print vectors of influence; if it doesn't, its effectiveness is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing requires cataloguing and policing of printers and existing books
rubrics_metrics.description: If executed, 'ye must repeal and proscribe all scandalous and unlicenc't books already printed... draw them up into a list... ordain that no forrein books be deliver'd out of custody, till they have bin read over' and 'catalogue all those Printers who are found frequently offending.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative-burden metric: quantify process for retrospective censorship, lists, custody, and printer monitoring. Consider resource and personnel implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing will stifle ministers' diligence and encourage doctrinal laziness
rubrics_metrics.description: If bold books cannot issue forth, 'it will concern [ministers] then to keep waking' — conversely, with licencing pastors may rely on printed sermons and become lazy, as 'penury he never need fear of Pulpit provision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional effect metric: evaluate whether censorship reduces incentives for clergy (or other professionals) to engage in original study and vigilance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing dishonours a nation by assuming all knowledge must be stamped
rubrics_metrics.description: To suppose the nation's understanding can be 'comprehended in any twenty capacities' and that knowledge should be 'monopoliz'd and traded in by tickets and statutes' is a disparagement of the whole nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National-reputation criterion: policy should not implicitly demean national intellectual capacity by centralizing approval in a small body.
